explanation.text: Read slider pᵢ as the chance that this position passes given that all earlier drafts passed. Later positions count only when their whole prefix survives, so multiply along each prefix before adding the survival probabilities. The leading 1 in the formula is the base output token every step produces regardless. Expected output divided by illustrative step time gives this demo’s effective throughput; it compares candidate lengths and does not predict production speed. In the reported results, a rank is one process in the distributed execution group, here usually one participating device.

blocks.title: Why separate the stages
blocks.text: A long prompt and a reply that has just started compete for the same device, yet need different resources. In [[prefill-decode|prefill and decode]], prefill computes the whole prompt at once and is often compute-bound; small-batch decode computes one new position per step and is often limited by [[bandwidth]]. [[pd-separation|Disaggregation]] gives each stage its own devices and its own scaling, and keeps long prompts from interrupting replies in progress. The cost is that state must move between the two groups.

blocks.title: How DeepInfer applies the separation
blocks.text: The DeepInfer Q&A deploys the vision encoder, prefill, decode and cache storage separately. The vision encoder turns images into [[embedding|embeddings]] for later computation; it usually runs on a single device and can scale with image traffic alone. For parallelism, the Q&A recommends EP2–8 / DP2–8 for prefill, as small as memory allows, and EP64–128 / DP64–128 for decode, as large as hardware allows. These ranges come from deployment experience; they do not follow from the compute-bound versus bandwidth-bound distinction.

blocks.title: Scenario: a follow-up about an image
blocks.text: A user uploads an image, asks for a description, then asks about one detail. By the second request, the image and the first turn have already been computed; as long as the [[prefix-cache]] survives, prefill reuses that prefix's KV and computes only the new question. If the follow-up attaches a new image, that image still goes through the vision encoder first. The resulting state moves to decode and the answer streams back. Which parts of the overview a request actually visits depends on what is new in it.

blocks.title: Deployable versus efficient
blocks.text: Running at all and running efficiently are different bars. The Q&A says a 1P + 1D deployment works, but in practice prefill and decode need roughly 1:1 device counts and decode is recommended at EP64 or above, so the efficient minimum unit is 64 prefill devices plus 64 decode devices. That number follows from decode's expert-parallel size; it is not the hardware floor for running the examples.

blocks.title: How reuse affects routing
blocks.text: The cache lives in an independent storage cluster, so every prefill machine can look up [[block-kv|Block KV]] for any prefix. Routing therefore need not send a conversation back to the machine that served it before and can choose by load alone; compute failures and scaling no longer take the cache with them. The storage chapter covers how prefixes are looked up and how KV reaches device memory.

blocks.title: From generation to the client
blocks.text: In decode, the system repeats forward then sample, producing new tokens for each request every round. Those tokens still pass through Recipe's stream parser before they become text, reasoning or tool-call events for the client. The next chapter puts this loop on a timeline to show where the CPU and GPU wait for each other.

blocks.title: Why the GPU waits for the CPU
blocks.text: A decode round has four steps: schedule(N) → forward(N) → sample(N) → post-process(N). Scheduling and post-processing are pure CPU work, and post-processing must wait for the GPU to sync the sampled result back. So while the CPU post-processes and schedules the next round, the GPU has nothing to do. Small decode batches have short compute steps, which makes that gap a large share of the time. Note that a [[kernel-launch]] only queues work on a [[cuda-stream]]; the call returning does not mean the GPU has finished.

blocks.title: Move waiting out of the critical path
blocks.text: DeepInfer's asynchronous scheduling staggers neighbouring rounds: while the GPU runs forward(N) → sample(N), the CPU runs schedule(N+1), launches forward(N+1), post-processes the older round N−1, then launches sample(N+1). The amount of work is unchanged and sampling still depends on the forward pass; the CPU work is simply hidden inside GPU execution time. The hard part comes from [[continuous-batching]]: requests leave and join every round, so a round prepared ahead of time must know which previous output belongs to whom.

blocks.title: Scenario: one request leaves and another joins
blocks.text: Suppose the previous batch was [A, B]; B has finished and this round is [A, C]. A can continue from its own previous output; C is new and has none. Matching by row position alone would attach B's output to C. The snippet below first compares request IDs row by row: if every row matches, row positions are reused as-is; if any differs, it builds a remap by looking up request IDs, and new requests with no match are marked as having no previous row and take the fresh-input path.

blocks.title: The limits of overlap
blocks.text: Overlap can only hide CPU work that fits within GPU execution time. Once the CPU side is slower, the GPU still waits for its next input. Raise the CPU workload in the demo below: even with async on, idle time reappears. The demo shows an ideal steady state without warm-up, drain or communication, so its idle share is not a measured device utilization.

blocks.title: Why some experts become busy
blocks.text: EPLB stands for Expert Parallel Load Balancing. In [[moe|MoE]], [[expert-routing]] picks experts by token content, not by which device is idle. Even after [[ep]] spreads experts across devices, a batch can concentrate on a few experts, and the devices holding them become stragglers. Because the [[all-to-all]] dispatch and combine wait for every device, one slow device stretches the whole round. A large number of experts therefore does not mean equal work per device.

blocks.title: Logical experts and physical locations
blocks.text: DeepInfer's answer is to give busy experts extra [[expert-replica|physical replicas]]: each device reserves some redundant slots, recent per-expert load decides which experts to copy into them, and placement is rebalanced periodically. One logical expert can have several physical instances with identical weights, so it does not matter which copy a token reaches. This is different from a [[shared-expert]], which is part of the model architecture; a replica is only a deployment copy.

blocks.title: Scenario: similar prompts arrive together
blocks.text: Imagine a batch of similar prompts that keep selecting E3. With only one copy, E3's device carries most of the work; add two replicas, E3′ and E3″, in other devices' redundant slots and those inputs split three ways. E3′ is a copy of E3, not a newly trained expert. Total work in the before-and-after drawing is unchanged; only its distribution moves. The real policy places experts from a statistics window and does not guarantee equal load in every round.

blocks.title: Observe and rebalance
blocks.text: The mechanism has three knobs: the statistics window sets how much history is observed, the rebalance interval sets how often placement changes, and the redundant slot count sets how many replicas fit. Prefill starts at 4 redundant experts per device, observes the last 100 steps and rebalances every 1000 steps; decode starts at 1 per device with a 1000-step window and a 10000-step interval, an order of magnitude longer than prefill. The table under the figure lists both sets.

blocks.title: Move weights with mappings
blocks.text: The policy code outputs a mapping from logical experts to physical slots, and the shuffle module moves the matching expert weights to their new locations. Mapping and weights must change together, or tokens reach slots holding the wrong weights. The snippet below is the policy's first step: divide each logical expert's windowed load by its replica count, then sort replicas by that per-copy load.

blocks.title: From placement to balance
blocks.text: The metric is moe_lb: the slowest rank's load divided by the mean load, equal to 1 when perfectly balanced. The Q&A reports 1.074 for prefill at EP4DP4, 1.045 at EP2DP2, and 1.090 for decode. In the figure, first check whether the busiest device dropped, then whether the others absorbed the extra work.

blocks.title: Which history must remain available
blocks.text: With long context, storing or recomputing every layer's state is expensive. Two ideas reduce the work. [[swa]] lets each position look only at a recent window, so that state has a fixed upper size. [[yoco]] lets later layers reuse the global KV produced by earlier layers instead of recomputing the whole input in every layer. Both of YOCO's layer groups are causal; this is not the translation-model split where an encoder reads the source and a decoder writes the target.

blocks.title: Then follow DeepInfer's CED
blocks.text: DeepInfer calls this structure [[ced|CED]], and this site keeps the Q&A's names: the earlier layer group is the encoder, the later one the decoder. The encoder computes all uncached input; the decoder's global KV, the [[block-kv|Block KV]], is projected directly from the encoder's final [[hidden-state]]. Each decoder layer also has its own SWA state, which cannot be projected and must be rebuilt by replaying recent tokens. There are two replays with different triggers and positions: the decoder replays the prompt tail on every prefill; the encoder replays one block before the matched boundary only when a prefix hit lacks SWA state.

blocks.title: Scenario: the prefix survives but window state does not
blocks.text: A user returns to a long conversation after a pause. Entrypoint finds Block KV for the prefix but no matching encoder SWA state. The hit need not be thrown away: keep the Block KV, move the hit boundary back one block, and recompute that block to restore SWA. Meanwhile the decoder replays the current prompt tail as usual. The SWA hit/miss switch in the lab below affects only the encoder side.

blocks.title: Decoder: replay the tail on every prefill
blocks.text: Top half of the main figure: input passes through the encoder, and the final hidden states are projected into purple Block KV that the decoder uses directly. Bottom half: on every prefill the decoder replays only the last 128 prompt tokens, with attention confined to that segment, so position i sees [max(s, i−127), i]. The result is an approximate SWA state used only for this decode and never stored in the prefix cache. Exact reconstruction would need 20 decoder layers over the final 2560 tokens; bounded replay nearly halves total prefill compute.

blocks.title: Encoder: recover at the prefix boundary
blocks.text: The lab below switches to the encoder. For an input of length L, the Block KV hit length L1 is at most L−134 (the 128-token window plus up to 6 tokens of speculative backtracking) and aligned to 128. If usable SWA state exists between L1−128 and L1, the hit stays at L1; otherwise it falls back to L1−128 and the last block is computed together with the uncached suffix. That block is recomputed only to rebuild SWA; its Block KV is reused, neither recomputed nor overwritten.

blocks.title: Which tokens can the query see?
blocks.text: In the lower part of the lab each cell is a token, and highlighted cells are the keys the current query can see. At the start of replay, the left edge is clipped by the start position s and few positions are visible; as the query moves right, the window grows until it reaches full size. The bar above answers where computation starts; this row answers what each step can see.

blocks.title: Why cache state has multiple homes
blocks.text: A [[prefix-cache]] saves recomputing repeated input, but if all state stayed in GPU memory, running requests would have no room, so the cache must be kept elsewhere. The two kinds of state behave differently: global KV can be reused across requests and grows with context; local [[swa]] state is bounded by its window, has a fixed size, and can be rebuilt by replay if lost. Two background concepts appear in this chapter: [[erasure-code|erasure coding]] adds encoded blocks so data survives some node failures, and [[gpudirect-rdma]] moves data directly between the NIC and the GPU, avoiding a detour through CPU memory.

blocks.title: Two paths for different state
blocks.text: DeepInfer's storage service is not open source, so every deployment mechanism in this chapter comes from the official Q&A. The two caches take two paths: [[block-kv|Block KV]] (Main KV and Indexer K) is persisted to an independent 3FS storage cluster; SWA state is not written to disk but stays in the memory of the machine that produced it, with an Entrypoint directory recording where. It is fetched across machines when needed and rebuilt by replay when it cannot be found.

blocks.title: Scenario: resume a conversation later
blocks.text: When a user pauses, the GPU memory held by that conversation can go to other requests. When the user returns, Entrypoint first finds the reusable prefix; Block KV comes back from 3FS, while SWA state is fetched if some machine still holds it in memory and rebuilt if not. The snippet below is a local function in the open-source engine that only shows how a window is read from a ring buffer: the logical position modulo the slot count gives the physical slot. It is not storage-service code.

blocks.title: From directory to device
blocks.text: The prefix lookup happens before routing: Entrypoint matches the prefix along a hash chain using metadata only, but routing needs the hit length first, so this step cannot overlap with compute. The actual data movement has two legs: a separate process copies KV from 3FS into host shared memory, then a thread inside the engine swaps it into device HBM via GDR. The second leg runs layer by layer and can overlap forward computation. GDR is used because the CUDA copy engine handles fine-grained KV blocks poorly; an RDMA NIC can saturate PCIe bandwidth without using any of the GPU's SMs.

blocks.title: Understand a read
blocks.text: 3FS stores data with 10+2 erasure coding: 10 data blocks plus 2 parity blocks per group, tolerating 2 simultaneous node failures. A read sends requests to 11 nodes in the group and decodes as soon as any 10 respond, without waiting for the slowest. “Request 11, use 10” is a read policy and is separate from the 10+2 encoding.

blocks.title: Fetch or rebuild SWA
blocks.text: The SWA path depends on Entrypoint's in-memory directory: logically one table, physically spread across Entrypoint hosts, it records which machine holds each SWA state. On a hit, state missing locally is fetched from another machine; if no machine has it, the system falls back to the bounded replay from the previous chapter. Either way, the goal is a usable local window for the computation that follows.

blocks.title: Keep state for later
blocks.text: Caches expire. The Q&A reports KVCache retention of 3 days for agent traffic and 7 days for chatbot traffic; reclamation is done by 3FS's own garbage collection, and kvcache-store has no expiry logic. These figures depend on DeepSeek's own storage capacity and access patterns and are not guarantees built into the open-source code.

blocks.title: Why request counts are insufficient
blocks.text: Every request counts as one conversation, yet their work can differ by orders of magnitude. Prefill work depends on input length, and long inputs are split by [[chunked-prefill]] into schedulable pieces; decode depends not only on how many requests are running but also on how long their [[kv-cache]] history is. Load balancing must therefore measure work, not count requests.

blocks.title: Illustration: equal counts, unequal work
blocks.text: For example, queue A holds two 100-token requests and queue B two 1000-token requests (illustrative values). The request counts match, but the positions to process are 200 versus 2000, so splitting by count does not split the input work. Real routing also considers cache hits and compute budgets, and this length ratio is not a latency ratio.

blocks.title: What the public estimator actually shows
blocks.text: The open-source repository has no load-balancing service, but it has a related component: a FLOPs estimator. It estimates attention, non-attention and logits work separately, which illustrates that a compute budget has to be broken down. It is only operation accounting, though, not the Q&A's fitted quadratic latency model, and it does no tier routing. Note that the snippet below returns (attention, total), where total already includes attention; callers must not add attention again.

blocks.title: Prefill: from tiers to chunks
blocks.text: Prefill assignment has three levels. First, requests fall into 4 tiers by total context: <16K, 16–64K, 64–256K and ≥256K, and each tier's share of machines is readjusted from its compute-quota demand in the previous round. Second, DP groups pull requests according to their remaining quota; since any machine can hit any prefix, there is no prefix affinity. Third, within a group each request goes to the rank with the lowest quota load. On a device, requests leave a FIFO queue, but the tokens processed per step are not fixed: the scheduler estimates time with a fitted quadratic cost(q, c), where q is this step's token count and c the already computed prefix, and solves for the largest q that stays within 32,768 tokens and exactly fills the remaining time budget.

blocks.title: Two decode dimensions
blocks.text: Decode balances two quantities at once: request count sets the batch size of each step, and total KV length sets attention cost. When two devices hold similar numbers of requests but one has much longer contexts, counting requests misses the difference. The Q&A's heuristic sends short requests to devices with lower concurrency but more KV, and long requests to devices with less KV.

blocks.title: Image work
blocks.text: The vision encoder uses yet another scale. The prefill machine picks a vision-encoder machine at random, and that machine hands the image to the device currently processing the fewest patches. Patch count follows directly from image width and height, so one image can cost more or less than another depending on its size.

blocks.title: Why output protocol belongs in the inference path
blocks.text: Users see text, tool calls or structured fields, while the model works on [[token]] IDs. On the way in, a [[tokenizer]] turns the conversation into tokens and [[special-token|special tokens]] mark roles and boundaries; on the way out, tokens produced one by one must be turned back into a valid protocol. When the output must follow a structure, [[constrained-decoding|constrained decoding]] restricts candidate tokens during generation instead of repairing the string afterwards.

blocks.title: Two components
blocks.text: Two components handle this part of the path. Protocol conversion and encoding belong to DeepSeek Recipe: it turns Chat Completions, Responses, Messages and other API requests into one conversation format before encoding, and parses output back into each protocol's streaming response. Recipe is open-sourced separately as deepseek-recipe, written in Rust with Python bindings, and its code is not in the DeepInfer repository. Structured output lives inside the DeepInfer engine: format constraints are compiled into a [[automaton|grammar automaton]] whose state advances at every step, and a [[token-mask]] blocks invalid candidates. A format constraint governs only form, not whether the content is true.

blocks.title: Scenario: a character and a marker span chunks
blocks.text: When streaming, the inference backend sends chunks at token granularity, and their boundaries need not fall on whole characters or tags. The character 中 takes 3 bytes in [[utf|UTF-8]]; the first two may arrive in one chunk and the last in the next. The parser must not emit garbage for the partial character, so it buffers until the bytes are complete. [[sse|SSE]] event boundaries likewise differ from network read boundaries. Tags can be split too: if the first half of the end-of-reasoning marker sits in an old chunk and the second half in a new one, incremental matching must remember how far it got. [[kmp|KMP]] uses a failure table to fall back to a prefix that can still match, instead of rescanning all earlier output on every chunk.

blocks.title: Keep the input structure
blocks.text: Encoding must tell apart two things that look the same. Special tokens inserted by the template, such as role markers, map directly to their token IDs; the same string typed by a user or returned by a tool, for example <｜User｜> inside a message, is encoded as ordinary text tokens, so text cannot inject control markers. And because special-token positions are known while the prompt is built, the plain-text spans between them can be encoded in parallel and joined in order, cutting tokenization time for very long contexts.

blocks.title: Constrain sampling
blocks.text: Structured-output compilation is decoupled from inference: format constraints (JSON schema, regex or EBNF) are compiled into grammar automata asynchronously on dedicated SO machines, and the result is retrieved before the request enters the engine. During generation the matcher advances the automaton with each output token, computes the set of legal tokens and applies a mask to sampling. The snippet below comes from this matcher: the constraint takes effect only after a trigger token sequence appears in the output, and the matcher recognizes that sequence token by token with a KMP failure table. The idea is the same as cross-chunk matching in stream parsing, but this is not Recipe's parser code.

blocks.title: Continue across chunks
blocks.text: Put together, the stream parser is a state machine that keeps its progress: a UTF-8 buffer handles incomplete characters, KMP keeps the delimiter-matching progress, and state records whether the current content is text, reasoning or tool arguments. Confirmed content is emitted at once without rescanning earlier text. Tool arguments need not wait for the whole object either: the tool name returns as soon as it is parsed, and arguments stream as JSON fragments along DSML boundaries.

reading.scope: Below are the source statements this chapter relies on. Diagram layouts and demo parameters are for explanation; take deployment settings from the sources.
takeaways: Distinguish special tokens from ordinary text.
Grammar constraints update valid candidates during generation.
Streaming parsers retain incomplete state across chunks.
reading.next: Next, relate input length and cache state to request workload.

blocks.title: Vocabulary first
blocks.text: The last chapter moves from the system into the model. A few terms first: a [[residual]] adds a sublayer's output back to its input; [[sparse-attention]] scores candidate positions and runs the main attention only on the selected ones; [[sinkhorn]] alternately normalizes a matrix's rows and columns. These are general definitions for reading the interfaces. This chapter follows the pinned code to show where data comes from and where it goes, without guessing at training motivations.

blocks.title: Reading order
blocks.text: The main figure reads top to bottom: first how the residual streams enter mHC mixing, then how the Engram side branch injects information into [[hidden-state|hidden state]]s, and finally how compressed KV and the indexer select and reuse state across layers inside attention. Every box maps to a code module you can open.

blocks.title: Trace one mixing operation
blocks.text: This model has not one residual path but several parallel residual streams. mHC combines them with a mixing matrix, which the code first passes through Sinkhorn normalization (sinkhorn_normalize) so that each row and each column sums to roughly 1. Mark the streams entering the mix, then follow the mixed result into attention and [[moe|MoE]].

blocks.title: Follow a side branch back
blocks.text: The Engram branch has three steps, each with its own inputs and outputs in the code: an [[ngram-hash|n-gram hash]] of consecutive tokens addresses a sharded table and fetches an embedding; a projection follows; a gate then fuses the result into the hidden states. It is a lookup inside the model, not retrieval from external documents.

blocks.title: Trace selection and reuse
blocks.text: Attention has two branches here: compressed KV and a sparse indexer. The indexer scores the compressed KV for each query and selects the top-k positions, and the main attention reads only those. A cross-layer topology object records three sharing relations separately: which layer the KV, the indexer K and the selected indices each come from; later layers (consumers) read from their source layers accordingly. Pick a consumer layer, find its source, then locate that reuse path in the figure.

blocks.title: Scenario: why shared indices are not enough
blocks.text: Suppose a later layer receives position indices selected by an earlier one. The indices alone are not enough: it also needs to know which KV they refer to and how to interpret the coordinates. Sharing indices therefore does not mean sharing the cache. The topology constructor below processes the configuration, builds each layer's source mapping and then validates it; these static relations are fixed before anything runs. Reading them first makes the runtime tensors much easier to follow.

blocks.title: Check the representation being used
blocks.text: Finally, keep data representations apart. [[fp8]] and [[mx]] describe how numbers are encoded and scaled, and different objects use different formats: the Q&A gives Main KV per-16 scaling with e4m3; Indexer KV and MoE routed-expert weights use per-32, ue8m0 MXFP4; SWA KV is stored as MXFP8. When you meet a low-precision field, first check which object it describes rather than assuming that everything named FP shares one format.

decodeLab.title: Decode lab: can guessing ahead save time?
decodeLab.intro: Once decoding is underway, another way to save time is to propose candidate tokens and verify them together. Having seen how a batch is scheduled, explore how DSpark chooses the candidates worth checking.
decodeLab.lead: Lower the confidence of an early position (say the second) and watch the positions after it stop being worth verifying. Then switch to fixed length and compare how the two strategies treat the same candidates.
decodeLab.scope: The sliders and timing curve explain a trade-off. Production allocates a shared budget across requests; official reported results are listed separately in the demo.

background.title: Draft first, then verify
background.text: Ordinary [[autoregressive|autoregressive generation]] selects an output before the next input is known. [[speculative-decoding|Speculative decoding]] proposes a draft first, then checks its known positions in parallel with the target. When weight movement dominates and spare arithmetic capacity remains, verification can approach the cost of a short decode step, but it is not always equally fast. [[acceptance|Acceptance]] determines how much draft survives; verification cost determines the time spent producing it. DSpark then asks how many candidates are worth verifying.

takeaways: Separate drafting from target verification.
Acceptance must be considered alongside verification cost.
The demo curve is illustrative, not a measured speedup.

basics.title: Before you start: from text to computation
basics.intro: Build a few small mental models before following a request into DeepInfer. Hover, click or focus a dotted-underlined term to open its definition.

questions.q: What work does a KV cache save?
questions.a: It saves recomputing old keys and values. Ordinary full attention still reads relevant historical [[kv-cache|KV]].

questions.q: Why allocate separate resources to prompt processing and generation?
questions.a: [[prefill-decode|Prefill and decode]] have different work shapes and typical bottlenecks. Separate resources reduce interference but require state transfer.

questions.q: Can any idle expert replace a busy expert?
questions.a: No. Different logical experts have different weights. An [[expert-replica]] provides another location for the same expert.

basics.kvTitle: Try it: how much KV does context need?
basics.kvScope: Illustrative values · Uncompressed full attention, one sequence, uniform layers; not a DeepInfer estimator. Read volume assumes one complete historical KV read per step, excluding weights, output writes and repeated kernel accesses.
basics.formula: Two (K and V) × tokens × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per element
basics.scope: Illustrative playback · Text is prewritten, not an actual tokenizer split or model prediction.

sections.title: What happens inside a conversation
sections.text:
Your text is first split by a [[tokenizer]] into [[token]] IDs, then an [[embedding]] turns them into vectors.

A forward pass moves those vectors through the layers; the internal representation passed between layers is a [[hidden-state]]. The last layer scores candidates for the next position, and [[sampling|sampling]] picks one token.

The chosen token is appended to the sequence and becomes the next input. Repeating this until an end marker or length limit is [[autoregressive|autoregressive generation]]. The player below shows the loop without running a real model.

sections.title: Why each step need not start again
sections.text: [[attention|Attention]] reads context through [[qkv|queries Q, keys K and values V]]: a query matches historical keys and combines the corresponding values. The [[kv-cache]] stores keys and values of processed positions. The next iteration adds new state while ordinary full attention still reads relevant historical KV. Continuing a conversation therefore need not recompute every old key and value. When compatible state survives between requests, a [[prefix-cache]] can reuse the same beginning. Matching means the same token prefix, not merely similar meaning.

sections.title: Process the prompt, then generate
sections.text:
[[prefill-decode|Prefill and decode]] are two work shapes of the same model. Every prompt position is known up front, so prefill computes them together. Decode handles 1 new position per request per step, and the next position waits for sampling.

Both read the weights on every forward pass. In prefill one read serves many positions, so arithmetic units stay busy. In a small decode batch one read serves few positions and history KV must be read too, so time goes to moving data and [[bandwidth]] becomes the limit.

This is a tendency rather than a rule: batch size, attention design and hardware shift the bottleneck. In MoE, a step reads only the selected experts' weights, though with a large batch the selected set approaches all experts.

sections.title: Experts are modules inside the model
sections.text: [[moe|Mixture of experts]] distributes part of the model computation among neural modules. [[expert-routing|Expert routing]] scores a token representation, selects top-k routed experts and combines their outputs; some architectures also use a [[shared-expert]]. Imagine several tokens all choosing one popular expert. Idle experts cannot simply substitute for it because they have different weights. The EPLB chapter explains how physical copies of the same expert help distribute that work. Expert identifiers and the number of connections in this drawing are illustrative.

sections.title: Split the data, or split the model
sections.text:
[[dp|Data parallelism]] gives different inputs to matching model replicas; [[ep|expert parallelism]] places different experts on different devices. ([[tp|Tensor parallelism]], which splits one layer's matrices, is not covered here.)

Under EP, tokens travel to the devices holding their selected experts and the results travel back. These two steps are [[all-to-all]] exchanges. The schemes can be combined: the DeepInfer Q&A describes attention DP together with MoE EP. The drawing below shows that combination for one MoE layer; device and expert counts are illustrative.

sections.title: Decide what kind of fast you need
sections.text:
Three questions come first: [[ttft|TTFT]] asks how soon a reply starts, [[tpot|TPOT]] how quickly it continues, and [[throughput]] how much work the system completes.

[[goodput]] also requires meeting latency objectives. High [[gpu-utilization]] only means a kernel was running for most of the measurement window; it does not prove the arithmetic units were saturated.

To read a performance plot, check the axis directions and workload first, then the [[pareto|Pareto front]]. Each point on the front is a tradeoff; none wins on every metric. Decide whether waiting time or total capacity matters more, then choose a point.

basics.kvParameters: An attention head uses its own query, key and value representations. KV head count is the number of key/value groups stored; head dimension is the number of values in each vector. Larger settings require more space for the same context. MiB is a binary unit of storage.
